column4: Whether speech is hidden or voiced, God knows ذات الصدور; this directly restages the section's movement from an audible exterior to the interior known by God.
أَلَا يَعْلَمُ مَنْ خَلَقَ answers a knowledge-question with the Creator's knowledge and names Him الْخَبِيرُ, the same question-and-answer structure that the section finds in 100:9-11.
On that day the human is informed of what he sent ahead and left behind; divine report supplies the complete outcome that the section says the human does not now grasp.
The human is بَصِيرَةٌ against his own self, a direct parallel to the person already seeing and witnessing his own condition in 100:7.
Even offered excuses cannot undo the self-witness of 75:14, sharpening the section's claim that the evidence lies before the human himself.
Tongues, hands, and feet testify against their owners on the judgment day; the ayah realizes both bodily self-witness and the source section's dictionary sense الشاهد اللسان.
After the bodily testimony of 24:24, people receive their due and know that God is the manifest Truth; the scene moves from involuntary witness to conclusive knowledge.
Hearing, sight, and skins testify to what their owners did, joining sensory organs, presence, and informing in exactly the threefold account of شهادة developed in the section.
People ask their skins why they testified against them, and the skins answer that God made them speak; the person's own exterior becomes an informed witness to the person.

They failed to hide from their own hearing, sight, and skins and wrongly supposed that God did not know much of what they did; this makes the gap between human concealment and divine knowledge explicit.
Their supposition about God's knowledge destroys them, stating the destination that the human in the section sees dimly but does not grasp in truth.
God creates the human and knows the whisper of his نفس while nearer than the jugular vein; the object of knowledge is the human's innermost self, not merely an external deed.
The ayah asks whether God best knows what is within all breasts after exposing a spoken claim of faith that collapses under affliction; outward profession and inward reality are distinguished.
The earth casts out its burdens, supplying the earth-and-graves side of the section's transition from scattered graves to disclosed information.
The earth tells أَخْبَارَهَا on that day; the same خ ب ر family as خَبِير makes the opened earth itself an informer.
The earth reports because its Lord has inspired it, identifying divine authorization behind the witness introduced in 99:4.
People issue forth separately لِيُرَوْا أَعْمَالَهُمْ, so emergence from the earth ends in being shown the deeds whose consequence they had not understood.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good يَرَهُ; the final scene turns the smallest formerly hidden act into something seen.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil يَرَهُ, completing the disclosure without allowing a hidden remainder.

Orphans are first tested and property is released only if guardians آنَسْتُم مِّنْهُمْ رُشْدًا; this is the exact source-section dictionary example in which sensing becomes knowledge of maturity through trial.
Moses says إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا and expects to return منها بِخَبَرٍ; one visible sign leads toward خبر, directly joining the section's ء ن س and خ ب ر senses.
Moses perceives a fire with آنَسَ and hopes to bring منها بِخَبَرٍ, repeating the concrete path from seeing to informed knowledge.
Moses says آنَسْتُ نَارًا and seeks guidance at it; this preserves the source section's secondary ء ن س sense of perceiving and its movement beyond sight toward knowledge.
Moses cannot be patient with what he has not encompassed خُبْرًا; the خ ب ر form names the missing grasp of the inner truth behind acts he will nevertheless see.
God says He will test people until He makes known the strivers and steadfast and tests أَخْبَارَكُمْ; trial, knowledge, and the خبر family meet in one formulation.
وَلَا يُنَبِّئُكَ مِثْلُ خَبِيرٍ makes the fully aware one the unmatched informer, directly joining the section's senses of inner knowledge and decisive report.
A confidential statement is disclosed, God makes it known, and the Prophet answers نَبَّأَنِيَ الْعَلِيمُ الْخَبِيرُ; hidden speech becomes report through the One who knows its interior history.
God suffices as witness between the parties and is بِعِبَادِهِ خَبِيرًا بَصِيرًا; witness, interior awareness, and sight are explicitly gathered around His servants.
Even a mustard-seed hidden in a rock or anywhere in creation is brought forth, for God is اللَّطِيفُ الْخَبِيرُ; hidden interior and eventual exposure are concrete.
Human beings do not know tomorrow's earning or place of death, while God is عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌ; it states the boundary between human ignorance of destination and God's complete awareness.
Every soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, followed by إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ; self-inspection and divine expertise occupy the same ayah.
God bears witness, along with angels and أُولُو الْعِلْمِ, to the truth of His oneness; testimony and knowledge converge in one decisive declaration.
God testifies to revelation sent بِعِلْمِهِ, the angels testify, and God suffices as witness; testimony is grounded in knowledge and communicated as decisive news.
The question أَيُّ شَيْءٍ أَكْبَرُ شَهَادَةً is answered by God as witness between speaker and hearers, exemplifying the section's شهادة as a conclusive report.
God says We are witnesses while people enter any deed, and not even an atom is hidden; present witnessing extends to complete knowledge of every scale.
Intercession belongs only to one who testifies to the truth وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ; the ayah expressly requires knowledge within valid testimony.
On resurrection God informs people of deeds He counted while they forgot them, and He is witness over everything; divine memory and report replace deficient self-knowledge.

God knows every secret conversation, is with its speakers wherever they are, and will inform them on resurrection; presence, knowledge, and informing reproduce the section's three components of witness.
Concealing testimony makes the heart sinful, and God knows what people do; spoken witness, hidden interior, and divine knowledge meet in one warning.

أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ أَمِ اللَّهُ confronts human knowledge, then condemns concealing testimony and says God is not unaware; it closely parallels the section's unanswered human question and divine answer.
Believers must be witnesses for God even against their own selves; it gives an ethical form to the person's inescapable testimony against himself.
Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what was earned; the self's own members supply the report that its tongue can no longer manage.
Each person's record is bound to him and brought out on resurrection as an open book, externalizing the truth of the person for inspection.
The person is told to read his own record and is sufficient that day as reckoner against himself; self-knowledge becomes unavoidable judgment.
God's record speaks about people with truth because their deeds were transcribed; the written trace becomes the decisive خبر-like witness to their history.
No word is uttered without an observer ready to record it, extending 50:16 from the unspoken whisper to the outward tongue and its preserved report.
Every soul arrives with a driver and a witness; judgment gives each person an accompanying testimony rather than leaving his condition private.
The covering is removed from prior heedlessness and sight becomes sharp; what was present but ungrasped is finally seen with full force.
The graves are overturned, an exact parallel to the grave-scattering condition attached to the knowledge-question in 100:9.
After the graves are overturned, every soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind; opened graves immediately become complete self-knowledge.
The day when secrets are tested and exposed directly parallels the extraction of what is in breasts before God declares His awareness.
On the day of presentation no hidden thing in the people remains hidden, stating the total disclosure toward which the section's progression moves.
On the near day a person sees what his own hands sent ahead; present action becomes visible outcome rather than merely abstract information.
Every soul then knows what it has brought, supplying the conclusive knowledge absent while the person merely witnesses his current condition.
People find every deed present in the book, which omits neither small nor great; the exteriorized record exposes the whole person without informational loss.
أَلَمْ يَعْلَم بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرَى reverses the section's question with an equally pointed one: does the human not know that God sees?
أَوَلَا يَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ مَا يُسِرُّونَ وَمَا يُعْلِنُونَ asks whether people know that God knows both their secret and public expression.
أَلَمْ يَعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ سِرَّهُمْ وَنَجْوَاهُمْ makes human failure to know God's knowledge of secret counsel the object of a question.
Those who think their secret and private counsel go unheard are answered that God's messengers beside them record it; hidden speech passes into witnessed report.
God knows the furtive glance of the eyes and what breasts conceal, moving within one ayah from the smallest visible act to the hidden interior.
Whether people reveal or conceal what is within themselves, God will call them to account for it; inward content itself becomes the object of judgment.
People are told that whether they hide what is in their breasts or reveal it, God knows it; the visible-hidden distinction cannot limit divine knowledge.
People fold their breasts and wrap themselves in garments to hide, yet God knows what they conceal and disclose; bodily concealment fails to cover the interior.
Whether speech is voiced or not, God knows the secret and what is still more hidden; knowledge reaches beneath the communicable exterior.
God knows what is spoken aloud and what people conceal, another direct statement that outward words and inward content are equally before Him.
The Lord knows what breasts conceal and what they reveal, naming the same interior/exterior pair on which the section's final knowledge turns.
The Lord knows what breasts conceal and what they declare, so the hidden person remains the object of divine knowledge.
God knows what people conceal and what they reveal despite their outward speech, preserving the distinction between human utterance and God's fuller knowledge.
God knows what people conceal and disclose and is knowing of ذات الصدور, giving both the outer/inner pair and the precise locus of interior knowledge.
God, His messenger, and believers will see deeds; then people return to the Knower of unseen and seen, who informs them of what they did. Seeing, knowing, and reporting form a full sequence.
After unavoidable death people return to the Knower of unseen and seen, who informs them of their deeds; God's report supplies knowledge beyond their present horizon.
Return to God is followed by His informing people of their deeds, for He knows ذات الصدور; report of actions is rooted in knowledge of the interior.
Human ingratitude, God's knowledge of ذات الصدور, return, and divine report of deeds all occur together, closely matching 100:6-11's movement from ingratitude to interior knowledge.
God knows people best from their first earthly formation and while they are embryos, so self-claims to purity yield to His knowledge of the whole person.
رَبُّكُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا فِي نُفُوسِكُمْ states directly that the Lord knows what lies within the selves addressed.
وَفِي أَنفُسِكُمْ أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ directs sight toward people's own selves, paralleling the self-evidence on which the section says the human is already a witness.
God will show signs in horizons and within selves until truth becomes clear, then asks whether His being witness over all things suffices; seeing oneself culminates in divine witness.

لَوْ تَعْلَمُونَ عِلْمَ الْيَقِينِ makes true knowledge the missing condition after worldly rivalry and the grave, directly echoing the section's question about grasping where one's visible condition leads.
لَتَرَوُنَّ الْجَحِيمَ states the eventual sight that follows the missing certain knowledge of 102:5.
ثُمَّ لَتَرَوُنَّهَا عَيْنَ الْيَقِينِ completes a progression from knowledge to unavoidable eyewitness certainty.
The trial is said to test what is in breasts and purify what is in hearts, followed by God's knowledge of ذات الصدور; experiential testing reaches the hidden interior.
The battlefield event occurs so that God may make the believers known, treating lived trial as a disclosure of real condition.
The same trial makes hypocrites known: they say with mouths what is not in hearts, while God best knows what they conceal.
People are not left merely to say they believe without being tested; outward statement must pass through experience that reveals its truth.
Testing makes the truthful and the liars known, directly illustrating the section's dictionary link between خبرة, اختبار, and knowledge of reality.
God will make the believers and hypocrites known, completing the testing-and-interior sequence surrounding the cited 29:10.
God creates the human in order to test him and makes him hearing and seeing; trial and the two senses named in the section stand at the beginning of human knowledge.
The hypocrites say نَشْهَدُ, God knows the proposition is true, yet God testifies that the speakers are liars; correct words are separated from the hidden truth of the witnesses.
Their hearts are sealed after belief and disbelief, identifying the inaccessible interior behind the testimony exposed in 63:1.
Their bodies impress when seen and their speech attracts when heard, yet they are likened to propped timber; seeing and hearing an exterior do not yield knowledge of the person within.
The Bedouins say with their tongues what is not in their hearts, and the ayah ends by calling God aware of their deeds; outward report and inward person diverge.
The Bedouins' spoken claim of belief is corrected because faith has not entered their hearts; the ayah distinguishes audible self-description from inner reality.
Hatred appears from mouths while what breasts conceal is greater, a precise outward sign/inner reality relation.
After private rage exposes the group behind its public face, God is said to know ذات الصدور; divine knowledge reaches what social observation only partly detects.
People relay the slander with their tongues and say with their mouths what they have no knowledge of; it is the direct opposite of a tongue serving as informed, decisive witness.
A report from an unreliable person must be verified lest people act بِجَهَالَةٍ; the ayah marks the boundary between mere خبر-like transmission and knowledge fit to ground judgment.
Jesus was witness over his people only while present among them, whereas after his removal God alone watched them; this clarifies human شهادة as presence and divine witness as unrestricted knowledge.
The brothers say they testify only to what they know and were not guardians of the unseen; the ayah explicitly limits valid human witness to knowledge and marks its boundary at hidden reality.
Eyes do not grasp God while He grasps all eyes, and He is اللَّطِيفُ الْخَبِيرُ; human sight's limit is set against divine subtle awareness.
Noah refuses to judge those whom others' eyes despise and says God knows best what is within their selves; visible social appearance cannot warrant a claim about inward worth.
Travel supplies eyes and ears, yet blindness belongs to hearts within breasts; sensory presence is explicitly separated from true understanding.
People know only an outward aspect of the nearer life while remaining heedless of the hereafter; partial exterior knowledge is distinguished from grasping where life leads.
People deny the signs although their own selves are inwardly certain of them; what the person knows within can be contradicted by his outward stance.
Hearts fail to understand, eyes fail to see, and ears fail to hear despite being possessed; the ayah defines the gap between sensory equipment and realized knowledge.
Some listen to the messenger, but the question denies that mere audition can make those who do not reason truly hear.
Some look at the messenger, but the question denies that mere looking can guide those who do not truly see.
People say they hear while they do not hear, turning outward reception into an explicit failure of inward apprehension.
Those who do not use reason are called deaf and dumb, reinforcing that sensory or verbal capacity is not the knowledge meant in the section.
Hearing, sight, and hearts did not benefit a people who rejected the signs; the organs that could lead toward knowledge remain ineffective without true reception.
One must not follow what one lacks knowledge of, because hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned; sensory evidence and accountable knowledge are joined but not equated.
At judgment the guilty say they have now seen and heard and ask to return; perception becomes certainty only after the missed consequence is present.
Jesus says God knows what is in his self while he does not know what is in God's self, defining the asymmetry between creaturely and divine interior knowledge.
The human asks what is happening to the convulsed earth; the question captures bewildered seeing immediately before the earth supplies its report in 99:4.
At judgment humans and jinn testify against themselves that they were unbelievers; their life-history becomes an adverse self-report.
At death the condemned testify against themselves that they were unbelievers, another scene in which the person's own condition yields the decisive testimony.
The idolaters are described as witnessing unbelief against themselves; their own public conduct makes their inner allegiance legible.
A witness is brought from every community and the messenger is brought as witness over his people; judgment is staged as informed testimony before God.
A witness is raised from every community and the messenger is brought as witness over his people, extending the judgment-day scene of presence and report.
The book is set down and prophets and witnesses are brought for truthful judgment; disclosed record and testimonial presence converge.
God knows every hidden key, falling leaf, grain in darkness, and wet or dry thing; the enumeration makes interior awareness concrete rather than generic omniscience.
God knows what enters and emerges from earth and what descends and ascends, detailing the خَبِير named in 34:1 as knowledge of things through every hidden passage.
After the people say they hear and obey, God is said to know ذات الصدور; an audible pledge is held beside knowledge of the interior that gives it truth.
God is Knower of the unseen of heavens and earth and knows ذات الصدور, directly extending knowledge from the inaccessible world to the inaccessible human interior.
In the context of fabricated speech, God knows what is within hearts and can erase falsehood and establish truth; interior knowledge adjudicates outward claim.
The One who knows all cosmic entering and emerging also knows ذات الصدور, placing the hidden content of persons among movements fully open to Him.
God knows what is within the believers' hearts and sends tranquility upon them; His action proceeds from the interior condition unseen by other people.
God knows the believers are truly worthy of the word of mindfulness and makes it bind them, in contrast to the visible zeal of ignorance around them.
Humans emerge from wombs knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts; the ayah lays out senses as the created path into knowledge.
God produces hearing, eyes, and hearts for people, the same sensory-to-interior faculties whose use the section probes.
After fashioning the human, God gives hearing, sight, and hearts; these stages supply the embodied beginning of the section's seeing-to-knowing progression.
The Creator gives hearing, sight, and hearts, shortly before 67:13-14 states His knowledge of breasts; human faculties and divine interior knowledge stand in deliberate proximity.
Those who forget God are made to forget their own selves; this is a specific failure of the self-knowledge demanded in 59:18 and in the section's human witness.
Worldly rivalry continues until people visit the graves, supplying the grave-bound destination before 102:5-7 contrasts deficient knowledge with certain sight.
Moses meets a servant taught special knowledge by God; this identifies the knower whose خُبْرًا exceeds Moses' grasp in 18:68.
The servant tells Moses not to question what he sees until the servant himself gives him a report about it, postponing judgment until informed explanation.
The servant promises to inform Moses of the interpretation of acts he could not bear, turning witnessed exteriors into knowledge of their inner reasons.
The damaged boat is explained as protection from a king who seized sound boats, revealing a beneficial interior purpose concealed by the visible damage.
The youth's case is explained through knowledge of what his unbelief and transgression would impose on believing parents, exposing an outcome unavailable to Moses' sight.
A replacement better in purity and mercy is named as the intended outcome, completing the hidden rationale begun in 18:80.
The repaired wall is explained by the treasure and righteous father beneath its visible surface, and the servant denies acting on his own; the inner face of the witnessed act is finally reported.
The hoopoe says it has encompassed what Solomon has not and brings certain news; presence elsewhere becomes knowledge communicated as a decisive report.
Solomon says he will see whether the hoopoe has told the truth, making a received report subject to testing before it becomes accepted knowledge.
A witness from the woman's household proposes a test of the shirt, so decisive testimony is tied to an observable sign rather than unsupported assertion.
The shirt torn from behind makes her accusation false and Joseph truthful; physical evidence exposes the inner history of the encounter.
When the husband sees the shirt torn from behind he draws the conclusion, explicitly moving from sight of evidence to knowledge of what occurred.
A speaker calls God to witness what is in his heart while his conduct makes him the fiercest adversary; claimed inward testimony and the person's true condition sharply diverge.
People say they believe with their mouths while their hearts have not believed and they eagerly listen to falsehood; speech and hearing expose no reliable knowledge of the interior.
The hypocrites fear a surah that will inform them of what is in their hearts, and God promises to bring out what they fear; concealed interior becomes disclosed report.

God has already informed the believers of the absentees' reports, will see their deeds, and will return them to the Knower of unseen and seen who informs them; report, seeing, knowledge, and final disclosure form one sequence.

Those who deny the Hour are answered by the Knower of the unseen, from whom not even an atom is hidden and in whose clear record everything remains; resurrection and exhaustive knowledge meet directly.
At judgment every soul knows what it sent ahead and is returned to God, so the person's history becomes fully known only at its destination.
God knows what people conceal and reveal, a repeated direct formulation of the section's exterior-to-interior movement.
Abraham addresses the Lord as knowing what people conceal and reveal and says nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from God.
The messenger's task is communication, while God knows what people reveal and conceal; human informing and divine interior knowledge are expressly distinguished.
In the setting of secretly extending affection to enemies, God says He knows what people conceal and disclose; the hidden allegiance behind an outward act is known.
Whether people disclose or conceal anything, God knows all things, restating the section's boundary between visible expression and divine knowledge.
God is the Manifest and the Hidden and knows everything; the ayah places outwardness, inwardness, and knowledge in one compact formulation.
The Prophet conceals within himself what God will disclose; the ayah directly stages an interior fact becoming outward under divine knowledge.
Joseph keeps a response within himself and does not reveal it to his brothers, while God is invoked as knowing their description; human concealment and divine knowledge are juxtaposed.
God knows what people harbor within themselves even when a matter is kept as a secret promise, making the self's unspoken content the object of knowledge.
God knows what lies in the hypocrites' hearts and commands speech addressed to their very selves; outward admonition is grounded in knowledge of their interior.
Humanity answers the primordial question with بَلَىٰ شَهِدْنَا so that no one can claim unawareness on resurrection; self-testimony is set directly against later ignorance.
The possible excuse that ancestors associated others with God cannot cancel the testimony of 7:172, paralleling the section's self-witness that survives offered excuses.
A witness is drawn from every community, the people are challenged for proof, and then they know that truth belongs to God; judgment moves from testimony to conclusive knowledge.
Believers must verify rather than tell a person offering peace that he is not a believer, and God is fully aware of deeds; human sight cannot safely pronounce on inward faith.
A lived test makes known who truly strives without hidden intimates besides God, and the ayah ends with God as aware of what people do; conduct discloses inner allegiance.
Reachable game serves as a test so that God makes known who fears Him unseen; trial exposes an inward fear that cannot itself be viewed.
The change of direction serves to make known who follows the messenger and who turns back; an observable response to trial discloses allegiance.
The question denies entry into the Garden before the strivers and steadfast are made known; trial reveals the reality behind aspiration.
Revelation, balance, and iron are given so that God makes known who supports Him and His messengers unseen; outward aid discloses an inward stance.
Death and life are created as a test of who is best in deed, supplying the experiential testing behind the same surah's declaration that the Creator is خبِير in 67:14.
The people of the Fire say that if they had listened or reasoned they would not be among its inhabitants; hearing joined to understanding would have grasped the destination they missed.
Some listen to the Prophet and then ask knowledgeable hearers what he just said; hearing has occurred without knowledge because their hearts are sealed.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best meaning are the people of understanding; this is a positive instance of hearing becoming discerning knowledge.
The person given his record in the right hand invites others to read it, turning his entire history into visible, communicable evidence.
He says he had known he would meet his reckoning, contrasting true prior knowledge of destination with the failure exposed in the section's question.
The condemned person had thought he would never return, precisely stating a failure to grasp where his visible life would lead.
The denial is answered that his Lord was always seeing him; deficient human forecast is set against continuous divine sight of the person.
At judgment there appears to the wrongdoers from God what they had never reckoned with; the consequence hidden behind their visible condition becomes manifest.
The evils they earned become visible to them and surround them, completing the movement from ungrasped outcome to inescapable sight.
The evils of people's deeds become visible and what they mocked surrounds them; an inwardly discounted destination becomes witnessed reality.
On the day every soul finds its good and evil deeds present, the person's moral interior history stands visibly before it.
What people had concealed before becomes manifest, a direct disclosure of hidden reality despite the false promise they then voice.
On the day a person remembers what he strove for, his own history returns as knowledge at judgment.
Hell is made plainly visible to everyone who sees, giving visible outcome to the remembered striving of 79:35.
When Hell is brought near, the person remembers, but the ayah asks what use that late remembrance can have; knowledge arrives only with the seen consequence.
The person wishes he had sent something ahead for his life, articulating too late the destination he failed to grasp beforehand.
God records what people send ahead and the آثار they leave, enumerating everything in a clear register; the person's full trace is preserved for later report.
A record speaks with truth and no soul is wronged; written evidence functions as the decisive report of the person's acts.
Everything people did is preserved in written records, preventing their own forgetting or concealment from erasing the truth.
Every small and great thing is inscribed, completing the records' exhaustive knowledge of a person's history.
God already knows the state people are upon, and on the day they return He informs them of what they did; knowledge concerns their condition before it becomes final report.
God takes people by night, knows what they commit by day, raises them until the term, and then informs them of their deeds; hidden life, knowledge, return, and report form a sequence.
Deniers of resurrection are told they will be raised and then informed of what they did; divine report answers their failed knowledge of destination.
The command to ask one who is خَبِير about the Creator presents the fully aware knower as the proper source of reliable report.
Public charity is good and hidden charity better, while God is aware of what people do; different visibility to humans does not change divine knowledge.
Some listen while coverings lie over their hearts so they do not understand and heaviness is in their ears; sensory presence fails to become knowledge.
Coverings over hearts prevent understanding and heaviness in ears prevents reception even while the recitation is heard, separating audition from inward grasp.
One reminded of God's signs turns away while coverings over hearts and heaviness in ears prevent understanding; visible and audible reminder does not ensure knowledge.
God knows what lies within breasts in the context of a dream-image that shapes courage and dispute; divine interior knowledge governs a limited human perception.
God's knowledge of good within captives' hearts determines a better gift, making hidden inward quality rather than visible captivity decisive.
The question asks whether the hearer knows that God knows all in heaven and earth and that it is in a record; human knowledge is redirected toward divine recorded knowledge.
People are told to leave both the apparent and hidden forms of sin because both will be recompensed; moral interior and exterior reach the same destination.
When people see divine punishment they finally profess belief and reject former partners; sight produces acknowledgment only after the outcome arrives.
Faith does not benefit them once they have seen the punishment, marking the boundary between timely knowledge and certainty forced by the final scene.
At the trumpet people rush from their graves to their Lord, continuing the grave-opening scene that follows the section's knowledge-question.
Those emerging ask who raised them, and the answer identifies the promised resurrection; bewildered perception precedes informed recognition.
